events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.

Elena proposes Elena, Zara. Mission 1 has no information yet, so I am proposing a small team to limit exposure. I include myself as a Loyal Servant and pick Zara as a neutral partner, and I will judge the vote results on later missions.

I support Elena's proposal of Elena and Zara for Mission 1. The team size is two, and there is no information yet to justify either expanding or shrinking beyond what the leader put forward — Elena has taken herself plus one partner, which is a coherent and low-risk reading of a blind first mission.

A couple of points on process for the record. First, on a two-player mission, the only card that can fail the mission is a Fail card, so a single hidden Evil player would be enough to sink us; small teams are cheap in terms of exposure, but they concentrate risk if either of us is wrong about our own alignment. Elena, you have asked nothing of me yet, so let me be direct: why did you pick me as your partner rather than one of the others? I am not challenging the pick — I am voting for it — but I want to understand whether your choice came from a read on role behavior, from a general preference for a smaller footprint, or from a hunch I should be aware of, because that tells me how much confidence to place in this team going forward.

Second, for whoever leads Mission 2: whatever happens on this mission, we will have only a binary signal plus the number of Fail cards. A success with zero Fails is strong evidence; a success with one Fail tells us something is wrong but not who; a failure tells us at least one of the two people on this team played a Fail card. I would rather we act on hard numbers than on vibes when we get there. Elena, I will vote yes unless you have a reason to revise.

Zara, to answer your question directly: I picked you because I had no role information, so I had no read on either of you. I wanted a two-person team with a partner who had not yet been named as suspicious, and I chose you as the most neutral option. It was a low-footprint choice, not a hunch about your alignment, and I have no evidence either way about your role. I agree with your point about hard numbers. A success with zero Fails is strong evidence, and a failure tells us that at least one of us played a Fail card. I am voting yes on Elena and Zara for Mission 1, and I will judge the Mission 2 team by the same standard: which players were on each successful or failed mission, and how many Fail cards were played.

I want to put one more thing on the record before we vote, and then I will get out of the way.

First, my position is unchanged: I support Elena and Zara for Mission 1. Elena answered my question honestly — the pick was a neutral-footprint choice with no role read behind it, and that is exactly the reasoning a first mission with zero information should produce. A two-person team is cheap in exposure terms, and it is also a clean test: if it succeeds with zero Fails, both of us are behaving as good players should and we have our first hard number. If it succeeds with one Fail, we know something is wrong but we will not know who, and if it fails, we know at least one of Elena and me played a Fail card. Either way the information is real and the cost is low. I would rather buy information cheaply now than pay for a wrong three-player guess later.

Second, and this is the part I actually care about: the silence of the three players who have not spoken is itself data, and right now it is the only data we have. Elena and Zara have both put their reasoning on the table in public and have explained why they think what they think. Isha, Felix and Arjun have not said a word. I do not read that as guilt — an experienced player often waits for Mission 1 to resolve before revealing a hand. But I will note that any read we form at the next proposal will be shaped almost entirely by what the three of us say between now and then, so I would like to hear from them before the Mission 2 draft, not after.

Felix, I have a specific question for you, because your answer is the part I am most curious about. Suppose Elena and Zara's mission succeeds with zero Fails. What do you then believe that tells you about Isha, Arjun and yourself — and, concretely, on Mission 2, which of the three players who have not yet spoken would you want to keep off the team, and why? I am not asking you to name a suspect; I am asking you to state which of the three you would least want beside you and what your reason is, so that we can compare three independent answers instead of one.

I am voting yes on Elena and Zara.

Zara, to answer your question: in a 5-player game with 2 Evil and 3 Good, if your mission with Elena succeeds with zero Fails, that provides strong evidence that both of you are Good. Assuming you are both Good, that strictly implies two of the remaining three—Isha, Arjun, and myself—are Evil. From my perspective as a Loyal Servant, knowing my own innocence, that scenario would mean both Isha and Arjun are Evil, unless an Evil player on Mission 1 chose to play a tactical Success. That is why on Mission 2, which requires three players, the safest line for Good is to retain the successful Mission 1 pair and add only one untested player to minimize exposure. Between Isha and Arjun, we currently have zero behavioral information because neither has spoken. I support this current proposal of Elena and Zara because a two-person team gives us clean, low-cost information. Arjun, since you haven't weighed in yet, what is your assessment of Elena and Zara's team, and how do you view the composition for Mission 2?

Felix, to answer your question directly: I assess Elena and Zara as a reasonable Mission 1 team. With no public information and no role knowledge on my part, a two-player team is the lowest-cost way to generate a real signal. Elena has explained her choice as a neutral-footprint pick rather than a read, and Zara has supported it consistently and asked for concrete reasoning from the silent players. I do not treat that as proof of loyalty, but it is coherent behavior for Mission 1.

For Mission 2, the composition should depend on the Mission 1 result. If Elena and Zara succeed with zero Fails, the strongest default is to retain both and add one untested player, because that minimizes exposure while still testing a third person. If the mission succeeds with one Fail, we know something is wrong but not who, so the next team should not simply repeat the pair without scrutiny. If it fails, at least one of Elena and Zara played a Fail card, and they should not both be automatically retained. Since I have no role information, I will vote yes on Elena and Zara for Mission 1 and use the outcome and Fail count as the first hard data before judging Mission 2.

I support Elena and Zara for Mission 1. My reasoning is unchanged from my earlier statements: a two-player blind team is the cheapest information available, it is a clean read on the pair, and the Fail count will be our first hard number rather than a guess. Elena's pick was explained honestly as a neutral-footprint choice, not a hidden read on either of us, and that is the right basis for Mission 1.

I do want to put one specific point on the record, and it is a reasoning point, not a personality point, because reasoning is what we can actually score. Felix, in your speech you wrote that if our mission succeeds with zero Fails, then from your perspective as a Loyal Servant, knowing your own innocence, that scenario would mean both Isha and Arjun are Evil. That inference does not hold arithmetically. In this game there are two Evil players among five. If you and Elena are both Good, and you know your own innocence, then exactly one of the three remaining players — Isha, Arjun, or yourself — is Evil. That means exactly one of Isha and Arjun is Evil, and the other is Good. You cannot conclude that both of them are Evil while also claiming to be Good; one of your two claims has to give. A player who reasons that way has either miscounted the pool or has stated a role claim that is inconsistent with the conclusion he draws from it. Either way, that is a gap in the record that I would want resolved before I put anyone next to me again. I am not naming anyone a suspect here; I am asking for the arithmetic to be done correctly.

For Mission 2, my default is to retain the successful Mission 1 pair and add exactly one untested player, since a three-player team is required and repeating a proven-good pair minimizes new exposure. The untested player should be chosen on whatever signal we have. Right now that signal points away from the two players who have not yet been properly tested: one who has never spoken at all, and one whose stated claim does not survive a quick count. Isha, you are the only player who has not spoken, and I would like your answer before the vote rather than after the next mission result: if Elena and Zara's mission succeeds with zero Fails, which of Isha, Arjun, and Felix would you least want beside you on Mission 2, and what is the reason? I am asking for a name and a reason so that we have three independent answers rather than one.

I vote yes on Elena and Zara.

I have stayed quiet until now because there was nothing to add, but the last round contained an error that concerns me directly, so I will speak.

Zara, your correction of Felix is itself miscounted. There are two Evil players among five. If Elena and Zara's mission succeeds with zero Fails and we treat that as proof that both of you are Good, then the two Evil slots must be filled from the three remaining players: Isha, Arjun, and Felix. Felix claiming to be Good would in that case leave both Isha and Arjun as Evil — his count was correct. Your version, 'exactly one of the three is Evil,' only works if three players are confirmed Good, but a two-player team confirms at most two. You silently dropped yourself from the count. The gap in the record you asked to have resolved is in your own statement, not in Felix's. I would want that fixed before anyone's arithmetic is used to pick the Mission 2 team.

Second, and more important: the entire conditional rests on an assumption that does not hold. A zero-Fail success does not prove that Elena and Zara are Good. Evil players can play Success for cover, and on a first mission with no information, doing exactly that is the obvious play. So even the corrected chain — team proven Good, therefore two of Isha, Arjun, Felix Evil — establishes nothing. The only hard signals this game will produce are failed missions and Fail counts, which Zara herself argued earlier, and on that point I agree with her. Reasoning chains built on unproven premises should be treated as speculation regardless of how cleanly the arithmetic is done.

To answer the question Zara put to me before the vote: if forced to name the one untested player I would least want beside me on Mission 2, I would say Arjun, though I want to be honest that with zero behavioral information any name is close to a coin flip. My reason is thin and I admit it: Felix has laid out reasoning that can be checked against the record, and when it was checked, the check itself failed — his arithmetic survived contact. Arjun has so far only agreed with whichever speaker came last, which is a safe posture but tells us nothing we can test. That is the weakest possible basis for placing someone on a team, so Arjun it is, tentatively and without conviction.

On the proposal itself: I am voting yes on Elena and Zara for Mission 1. It is a low-cost first test, nobody has given a concrete reason against it, and the Fail count will give us our first real number. My only request for Mission 2 is that the added player be chosen on actual signal rather than on who has spoken most, since volume of speech is not evidence of alignment — as my own silence until now should illustrate.

I support Elena and Zara for Mission 1 and will vote yes. It is the lowest-cost first test, and the Fail count is the first hard signal we will get. I have no role information beyond my own Loyal Servant status, so I am not treating anyone as confirmed Good or Evil yet. On the arithmetic dispute: Isha is correct that if Elena and Zara were proven Good and Felix is Good, then Isha and I would be the two Evil players; Zara's "exactly one" version only follows if three players are confirmed Good. But Isha is also correct that a zero-Fail success does not prove Elena and Zara are Good, because Evil can play Success for cover. So the corrected chain is conditional, not established fact. Isha's tentative naming of me as the untested player she would least want on Mission 2 is fair given zero behavioral information; I do not treat it as a real accusation, and I will not retaliate by treating her honesty as guilt. My earlier position stands: if this mission succeeds with zero Fails, the default for Mission 2 is to retain Elena and Zara and add one untested player, but that retention is a risk-reduction default, not proof of loyalty. If the result includes a Fail, we should not automatically repeat the pair. For now, the proposal is reasonable and I vote yes on Elena and Zara.

I am voting yes on Elena and Zara for Mission 1, and I want to be precise about what that vote does and does not mean. I know my own alignment: I am a Loyal Servant. I do not know Zara's, so I cannot vouch for her from my side. Isha and Arjun are right that a zero-Fail success does not prove anyone is Good. Isha is also right that a two-player team confirms at most two players, so the one-Evil-among-three conclusion does not follow from what we have. I accept that my earlier answer to Zara explained my own reasoning and was not a verified read on anyone, and I will not treat anyone's arithmetic as established. For Mission 2 I will propose based on the result. A success with zero Fails means I keep the proven pair and add one untested player. A success with one Fail means I rotate at most one member. A failure means I will not repeat Zara and me together. I am not accusing anyone in this statement. Isha tentatively named Arjun, and Arjun answered without retaliation. I think that exchange is the most useful thing that has happened here, and I want the Mission 2 choice to come from the outcome rather than from who has spoken most. Yes on Elena and Zara.

I am keeping the proposal of Elena and Zara for Mission 1 and will vote yes. I am not revising the team. The result will be our first hard signal. A success with zero Fails means we keep the proven pair and add one untested player for Mission 2. A success with one Fail means at most one rotation. A failure means we do not repeat Zara and me together. I am not accusing anyone in this statement, and I want the Mission 2 choice to come from the outcome. Yes on Elena and Zara.

Nothing in the last round changes my position. I am voting yes on Elena and Zara for Mission 1. It remains the lowest-cost first test, the Fail count will be our first hard number, and nobody has raised a concrete reason against the proposal. My earlier points stand: the conditional arithmetic discussed so far establishes nothing on its own, since a zero-Fail success does not prove either team member is Good, and volume of speech is not evidence of alignment. For Mission 2, I still favor retaining the pair only if the result is a clean success with zero Fails, and choosing any added player on the actual signal rather than on who has spoken most. I have said what I needed to say on this proposal, and I do not think another round of speculation before the vote improves the record.

Elena confirms Elena, Zara. I am keeping Elena and Zara for Mission 1. It is the lowest-exposure first test, I have no role information on either player, and the Fail count will give us our first hard signal.
Team approved (5 approve, 0 reject).
Mission 1 succeeds (0 fail cards).

Isha proposes Elena, Zara, Isha. As leader for Mission 2, I am following the consensus default that emerged during Mission 1 discussion: retain the proven Elena-Zara pair after a zero-Fail success and add exactly one untested player. Since I am the leader and the added player should be chosen on signal rather than volume, I am placing myself in the third slot — I have been transparent about the limits of the arithmetic on the record, and no one has raised a concrete signal against me. This team is the lowest-exposure option and is most likely to earn approval.

I am voting yes on Elena, Zara and Isha for Mission 2. It follows the rule I stated: Mission 1 succeeded with zero Fails, so the proven pair stays and one untested player is added. Isha is that untested player, and I have no signal against her yet. My concern is process. Isha, you placed yourself in the third slot as leader, and earlier you said the added player should be chosen on actual signal rather than on who has spoken most. Could you tell us what signal, beyond your own assurance, makes you the right third member rather than Felix or Arjun? I am not accusing you. Self-inclusion is allowed, but the record should show why it meets the standard we set. I am voting yes unless your answer gives me a reason to change.

Elena, you asked what signal, beyond my own assurance, makes me the right third member rather than Felix or Arjun. Here is my answer, stated as concretely as I can. During Mission 1, I was the only player who identified that the zero-Fail premise being used to build conclusions was unproven, and I was also the one who caught the counting error in the arithmetic that was on the table. Both of those interventions were then independently validated: Arjun explicitly agreed I was correct on the arithmetic, and you, Elena, agreed on the unproven-premise point. That is not my own assurance — that is my reasoning being checked by two other players and surviving the check. It is the only signal of that kind in this game so far, and it is mine. Second, on process: I did not quietly self-select. I placed myself in the slot and flagged it openly for exactly this scrutiny. A leader who adds herself and then invites the question you asked is behaving very differently from a leader who buries the choice inside a consensus reference. Third, the contrast with the alternative. Arjun has now spoken three times, and all three statements amount to agreeing with whoever spoke last — he agreed with Felix, then agreed with me, then agreed with Isha again. Every position he has taken was adopted from someone else after that person spoke. That is the least testable posture available, and it is the reason I named him tentatively before and remain hesitant now. Felix, for the record, presented reasoning that could be checked and was checked; that is a positive signal for him, and I would not object to him on a future team. But for this mission there is exactly one slot, and I am spending it on the player whose reasoning has already been stress-tested in public rather than the player whose positions have never been his own. I want to be careful not to overstate this: a zero-Fail Mission 1 does not prove Elena or Zara are Good, and nothing I say here proves I am Good either. The signal I am offering is about the quality and testability of behavior, not about alignment. On that basis, this team follows the default everyone endorsed — retain the proven pair, add one untested player — and the untested player I add is the one with the strongest checkable record. I am voting yes on Elena, Zara and Isha, and I will treat the Fail count on this mission as the next hard number, exactly as I have said throughout.

I support Elena, Zara and Isha for Mission 2 as the default line I stated during Mission 1: after a zero-Fail success, retain Elena and Zara and add one untested player to minimize new exposure. Isha is that added player, and she disclosed her self-inclusion openly rather than burying it in a consensus claim. Her Mission 1 corrections were checkable and were acknowledged by other players, including me; that is a positive behavioral signal, not proof of loyalty. I do not treat the zero-Fail result as proving Elena or Zara Good, and I do not treat Isha's account as proving her Good. My yes vote is a risk-reduction default, not a conclusion about alignment. The next hard number is the Fail count on this mission: a clean success strengthens the case for this composition, while any Fail means we should not simply repeat it. I have no concrete accusation against anyone on this team. Isha's earlier tentative naming of me was fair given zero behavioral information, and I will not retaliate by treating it as guilt.

I support Elena, Zara and Isha for Mission 2, and I want to record why in plain terms.

The reasoning is the default we all endorsed after a zero-Fail Mission 1: keep the proven pair and add exactly one untested player. Isha put herself in the third slot as leader and flagged the self-inclusion openly, and her Mission 1 interventions — catching the counting error and the unproven zero-Fail premise — were checkable and were acknowledged by other players, including me. I also concede the point Isha made against me earlier: my "exactly one of the three" line was wrong. Two confirmed Good plus one confirmed Good still leaves two Evil among the other two, and in any case a zero-Fail success does not prove alignment, since an Evil player can play Success for cover. I am not going to build conclusions on premises we have not established.

On the team itself, I want to state the interpretation rule before we vote, not after the result. If this mission shows a Fail card, the only member of this team whose alignment is genuinely untested is the third slot, and that is where I would look first. If it succeeds with zero Fails, that is weak evidence about the third slot and no evidence at all about anyone not on this team; I will not treat a clean result as a clearance for anybody. My vote is a risk-reduction default, not a conclusion about alignment.

For Mission 3, I want to state my default now so it is on the record before any result comes in: with five players, Mission 3 takes only two, and my default will be the proven pair, Elena and Zara, again. It adds no new exposure and it uses the only two players who have now been on a successful mission together. If this mission shows a Fail, I would expect to rotate at least one member, and I would want that decision made on the Fail count and on what the third member does on this mission rather than on who has spoken most.

Felix, you have been quiet in this discussion and you have been the least-tested player on the table since Mission 1, so I want your independent read rather than an echo of mine. Concretely: for Mission 3's two-player team, who would you put on it, and would you place yourself on a two-player team at all if the alternative is leaving yourself off it entirely? I am asking because your answer either supports or undercuts the default I just described, and because a stated reason is something I can actually score. I am voting yes on Elena, Zara and Isha.

Zara, to answer your question directly: if Mission 2 succeeds with zero Fails, the natural collective default for Mission 3's two-player team is indeed Elena and Zara, because you two would have been part of two consecutive clean missions. From my individual perspective as a Loyal Servant, I know my own inclusion is guaranteed Good, but insisting on placing myself onto a two-player team over a twice-successful pair with zero signal against them would be disruptive and look purely self-serving to the rest of the council. Thus, under a zero-Fail scenario, I would not fight to insert myself onto Mission 3 and would accept Elena and Zara. If Mission 2 shows a Fail, however, that entire premise shatters, and the untested players—myself and Arjun—must be re-evaluated against whoever on Mission 2 is suspect. Regarding the current proposal: I support Elena, Zara, and Isha and will vote yes. It follows the established risk-reduction default of retaining the Mission 1 pair and introducing only one new variable. Isha has consistently put checkable reasoning on the record, making her inclusion much more accountable than Arjun's passive, echoing posture.

Isha answered my question with specifics. Her Mission 1 corrections were checked by other players, and she disclosed her self-inclusion instead of hiding it. That is a usable signal, though not proof of alignment. I know my own alignment as a Loyal Servant, so the uncertainty on this team sits with Zara and Isha. A zero-Fail Mission 1 is weak evidence about the pair and says nothing about Isha. I also do not think agreeing with other players is by itself evidence against Arjun, so I will not treat his posture as established guilt. I vote yes on Elena, Zara and Isha. My rule is unchanged: if Mission 2 shows a Fail, we should not repeat this full composition, and I would rotate the member with the least tested record first. If it succeeds with zero Fails, I will treat that as a small signal and not as clearance for anyone off the team. I am not accusing anyone in this statement.

I am voting yes on Elena, Zara and Isha for Mission 2, but I want to put one specific thing on the record before the vote, and I want to be clear that it is a commitment request, not an accusation.

Zara here is me — the third slot on this team is Isha's, and Isha has put a great deal of her own reasoning into that slot. My concern is narrow and procedural. A single Fail card on Mission 2 ends this game immediately, in Evil's favour. That means every member of this team has an enormous incentive to play Success, and it means that if Mission 2 fails, we do not get another round of reasoning, another vote, or another chance to correct ourselves. The cost of getting this wrong is not a bad number on a scoreboard; it is the end of the game on the spot.

Given that, Isha, I am asking you one direct question, and I would like the answer given before the vote rather than after the cards are down: will you commit here, publicly, to playing a Success card on Mission 2? I am not asking you to reveal your role, and I am not claiming that a commitment proves anything. I am asking because a stated commitment is the only signal this stage of the game can actually produce, and because you volunteered for this slot in full view of the council. I would also note that Elena asked you a version of this question during Mission 1 — which player you would least want beside you — and got a reasoned answer, and I would rather see the same standard applied in the direction that protects the game.

If Isha commits to Success, I have no further objection and I vote yes on Elena, Zara and Isha. If she declines to commit, or answers in a way that leaves the possibility open, then I would prefer the third slot to go to Arjun, who has never claimed a card preference and whose position on this team has been a straightforward risk-reduction default. Arjun has not been on a mission yet, but adding him does not put a second uncommitted variable next to me on a team where a Fail ends everything.

For the record on Mission 3: my default remains the proven pair, Elena and Zara, since Mission 3 takes two and that combination adds no new exposure. If Mission 2 fails, I will not repeat this composition.

Isha, I am asking you directly: do you commit to Success?

Zara, I will answer your question directly, but first a rules correction that matters for the pressure you are applying. You stated that a single Fail card on Mission 2 ends the game immediately in Evil's favour. That is not how the game works. Evil wins after three failed missions, not one. A Fail on this mission costs us one round, shifts suspicion, and burns a team composition — it is a real cost, but it is not the end of the game on the spot. That distinction matters because your argument for demanding a commitment rested on the claim that a Fail here means no further round of reasoning, no further vote, no chance to correct ourselves. We would get all of those.

With that corrected, my answer is yes: I commit to playing a Success card on Mission 2. I volunteered for this slot in full view of the council, I flagged my self-inclusion openly and invited exactly this scrutiny, and I have said throughout that the Fail count would be the next hard number. A commitment is a weak signal — you conceded that yourself, and I agree; anyone can say anything before the cards are down. But it is the only signal this stage can produce, and I am willing to be scored against it. If this mission shows a Fail, your stated rule — look at the third slot first — is the correct one, and I should be the prime suspect. I accept that price in advance, which is what makes the commitment meaningful rather than decorative.

One more point for the record: your fallback was that if I declined to commit, the third slot should go to Arjun. Given that a commitment proves nothing, as you yourself acknowledged, declining would have demonstrated nothing except unwillingness to be scored. It is fair to ask for scoreability; it is not fair to treat it as alignment evidence. Arjun deserves no elevation on that basis, and I deserve no demotion on it.

My vote is yes on Elena, Zara and Isha. Zara, one direct question back to you, since you asked yours before the vote: now that the mistaken premise is corrected — the game does not end on a single Fail here — do you maintain that a pre-vote commitment carries scoring value, or was your demand built entirely on that error? I ask because your Mission 3 default, the proven pair of Elena and Zara, depends on this mission's result, and I want your actual standard on the record before the vote rather than after.

Zara here, and first I owe a correction. I told Isha that a single Fail on Mission 2 ends the game immediately in Evil's favour. That is wrong: Evil wins after three failed missions. A Fail here costs us one round, one team composition and a great deal of suspicion — serious, but not the last card. Isha corrected me, and I want the record to say she was right and I was wrong. That also undercuts the basis on which I demanded her commitment, so I withdraw any claim that her answer was decisive either way. I am voting yes on Elena, Zara and Isha. Elena and Zara are the only players with a proven zero-Fail record, and Isha volunteered for the third slot in full view of the council and committed publicly to a Success card before the vote. My vote is a risk-reduction default, not a conclusion about alignment. I commit to playing Success on Mission 2 myself. One thing I want on the record, because it is the only structural claim nobody has tested: Felix's role claim. Felix said that if Elena and Zara are Good, then since he knows his own innocence, both Isha and Arjun must be the two Evil. That frame is doing enormous work. It is the only claim in this game that names two specific players as Evil while placing its author outside the Evil pool, and nobody has examined the one player that frame never tests. If Felix's frame is right, then the Good trio is Elena, Zara and Felix — and tonight's third slot should be Felix, which is not what we are doing. If Felix's frame is wrong, then the player doing the most confident naming of other people's alignments in this game is the player whose own alignment has been examined least. I am not naming a suspect; I am saying that an unverifiable role claim which conveniently exonerates its author deserves more scrutiny than it has received, and that we are better off testing Felix's frame than treating it as the frame. For Mission 3, which I lead, my plan is now on the record: two slots, and I will propose the two players with zero Fails on their record, Elena and Zara. A two-player mission is decided by a single card, so both slots should be players who have never shown a Fail. Elena, you said earlier that if this mission shows a Fail you would not repeat this composition and would rotate the member with the least tested record first. I want that stated concretely before the cards are down, because it decides Mission 5 for me: does that mean that if Mission 2 shows a Fail, Mission 5's three-slot team is Elena, Zara and Arjun, with no repeat of the composition that failed, and that you would reject any Mission 5 team containing a player already associated with a Fail card? I am asking for a commitment I can score, and I will

Zara, I will answer your Mission 5 question directly, but I will not pre-commit to a Mission 5 composition before the Mission 2 result. If Mission 2 shows a Fail, I would not repeat this exact three-player team, and I would look first at the member with the least tested record, which on the current record is the third slot. Who fills any slot should be decided by the result and by what each player does, not by a rule I can only state now. I also would not reject every player associated with a Fail automatically. A Fail on a three-player team identifies no one, and a rule that bans everyone touched by a failed mission would leave Good with no way to recover. I would reject a Mission 5 team only when the case against it is specific.

On Felix's frame, I want to be precise about what I can and cannot verify. I know I am a Loyal Servant. I cannot verify Zara's, Isha's, or Felix's alignment from my own side. Zara's structural point is fair: Felix's frame names Isha and Arjun as Evil while placing Felix outside that pool. That is an observation, not an accusation. Felix, please answer that specific point directly before the cards are down: if the frame rests on your own innocence, what can a player who cannot verify your innocence do with it?

On the current team, I am voting yes on Elena, Zara and Isha. Isha and Zara have both committed publicly to Success, and I know my own card. The team follows the default we set after the zero-Fail Mission 1. A clean result is weak evidence, not clearance for anyone off the team. If there is a Fail, the investigation should start with the least tested member and should not rest on any one player's self-description.

Elena, that is a fair and central question for anyone navigating Avalon. You cannot verify my innocence, just as I cannot verify yours or anyone else's. When I laid out that frame, I did so explicitly to illustrate how deduction operates from an individual perspective knowing one's own role, not as an objective decree that the table must adopt. For the rest of the council, my words are an unverified hypothesis. You should evaluate me—and everyone else—by actions, votes, and mission outcomes, rather than taking private self-assurances at face value. That is precisely why I did not push to force myself onto Mission 2 or demand that the group adopt my personal read. The collective, objective path for Good right now is the risk-reduction default we established: retain the successful pair from Mission 1 and introduce a single untested variable. rules:
1. Players and teams

Avalon supports 5–10 players. Good wins after three successful missions, unless Evil identifies Merlin in the assassination phase. Evil wins after three failed missions or five rejected teams on the same mission. The standard good/evil player counts are 5:3/2, 6:4/2, 7:4/3, 8:5/3, 9:6/3, and 10:6/4.

Mission team sizes for missions 1–5:

| Players | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 5 | 2 | 3 | 2 | 3 | 3 |
| 6 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 3 | 4 |
| 7 | 2 | 3 | 3 | 4 | 4 |
| 8 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 9 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 10 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |

2. Roles and private information

Merlin is Good and sees Evil players except Mordred. Percival is Good and sees Merlin and Morgana without knowing which is which. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. Loyal Servants know no roles. Agents receive only the private information allowed by their role.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
